vignette:
Arjun was driving home from his editing shift at the digital media company just past midnight when the patrol car's lights flashed in his rearview mirror. He pulled over, heart already thumping, and did everything he thought would keep him safe-hands on the wheel, window down, movements slow. But the male officer who approached the driver's side was already shouting; the female officer who appeared at the passenger door was quieter, her voice cold and flat. Within minutes he was out of the car, face pressed against the cold asphalt, wrists yanked behind his back and locked into cuffs. The pavement was bitterly cold against his cheek, the metal of the handcuffs biting into his skin. He lay there, body stiff and helpless, while the female officer's boots stood inches from his face. He could smell the faint, cloying perfume from her uniform, mixed with the mustiness of the patrol car's interior when they finally put him inside. He was released without charges after three hours, but something in him had already been taken.

For weeks afterward, Arjun found himself unable to shake the physical imprint of that night. When he sat at his desk in the office, his hands would sometimes drift behind his back as if searching for cuffs; he would catch himself and pull them forward, but the sensation lingered-his body felt locked in that same prone position, cheek against an imaginary cold floor. The grief that came with the memories was the hardest part to explain. It wasn't just fear or anger; it was a raw, overwhelming grief, as though someone he loved had died. He had lost something that night, though he couldn't name it-perhaps his sense of being a person who could move through the world without suspicion, or the belief that the world was fundamentally fair. That loss hollowed him out. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. His work as an editor, once a source of pride-shaping stories, catching inconsistencies-now seemed pointless. He stared at manuscripts for hours, the words blurring, and asked himself why it mattered. He had come to believe that his inability to shake the event proved he was a lousy coper. Other people endured worse and moved on. He could not, and that failure confirmed that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The future felt closed, a door that had been locked from the inside.

The triggers surfaced in small, crushing moments. The cold of the office air-conditioning made him flinch; he began wearing long sleeves even in summer, and when his wife Priya touched his skin with a cool hand, he would jerk away. He avoided the temperature-any temperature-that reminded him of that pavement. More puzzling to him was his reaction to being alone with women. At work, he found himself requesting that a male colleague join meetings with female freelancers, and he made excuses to avoid one-on-one catch-ups with his female manager. He did not fully understand why-it was not that he feared women generally-but the quiet intimacy of a closed room with a woman felt dangerous, reminiscent of the female officer's cold competence as she watched him on the ground. And then there were the moments of dissociation: a sudden onset of unreality, as if he were watching himself from a distance, the world going thin and dreamlike. Those episodes terrified him because they often heralded a full memory rush. He would smell that perfume again, or the musty car interior, and his body would lock into the same rigid position on the floor of his living room, grief flooding in.

Over the months, avoidance became a way of life. He stopped driving after dark altogether, taking the subway home even though it added forty minutes. At home, he kept the thermostat high, and he pulled away from Priya's touch at night, claiming he was too tired. She grew hurt and confused; their conversations narrowed to logistics. At work, his reluctance to interact with female colleagues was noticed. His manager, a woman, asked if there was a problem. He mumbled something about anxiety, but the tension grew, and he was passed over for a promising project. The consequence of protecting himself from every trigger was a shrinking existence-a life in which he felt like a ghost haunting his own circumstances. The grief deepened.

It was Priya who finally insisted he talk to someone. She had found him one evening, sitting on the cold tile floor of the bathroom, hands behind his back, tears streaming down his face. He could not explain what had happened; he had simply felt the unreality seep in, and then the smell, and then his body had taken over. He agreed to therapy because he was terrified of losing her, but underneath that fear was a deeper one: that he was right, that nothing good could happen to him anymore, and that even therapy would only prove how broken he was. He came to the first session with his shoulders tight, his eyes wary, his hands clasped in his lap-carefully, deliberately, in front of him.
